context_blurb:
Switch on a flashlight in a dark room, and a beam shoots across to the far wall. Light is always on the move. It bounces off things, bends as it passes into water or glass, and gets soaked up by dark things. Everything you see, you see by light.

Light travels in straight lines, and it never curves round a corner on its own. Test it with a flashlight and three cards. Punch a small hole in each card and stand them one behind another between a wall and the flashlight, with all three holes lined up. A bright dot appears on the wall. Nudge the middle card a little to one side, and the dot disappears from the wall. No straight path runs through all three holes any more, and light cannot bend round the card.

Straight lines explain shadows too. A cardboard cat held in a lamp's beam blocks the light that hits it, while the light just missing its edges flies straight on to the wall. A shadow has the same shape as the thing that casts it, because light travels in straight lines. It is simply a place the light cannot reach.

The Sun and a lamp give out their own light, but most things give out none. A chair or a book is seen only because light bounces off it, and some of that light travels straight into your eyes. Your eyes send out no light; they only take it in. In a room with no light at all, you would see nothing.

Light that bounces off a thing is reflected, and nearly everything reflects some light, not just shiny things. A mirror is so smooth that it sends light back in neat order, so you see a sharp image in it. White paper is rough on a tiny scale, covered in bumps too small to see. Paper reflects plenty of light, but its bumps bounce that light off in every direction, so no picture forms. That scattered light is how you see paper, and almost everything else.

Light can bend, too. It travels more slowly in water and glass than in air, so it changes direction as it passes from one into another. This bending is called refraction. A straw in a glass of water, seen from the side, seems to snap in two where it enters the water. Light from its underwater part bends as it goes from water into air on its way to your eye, which shifts where that part seems to be. Lift the straw out, and it is perfectly straight. A lens is a piece of curved glass that bends light by refraction, and a magnifying glass is one: a small beetle seen through it looks bigger than it is.

Sunlight looks white, yet it is a mix of many colours. A prism, a block of clear glass with slanting sides, bends each colour by a different amount, so it spreads sunlight into a band of colours from red to violet. Isaac Newton turned a second prism the other way, and it gathered the colours back into white light: they had been in the sunlight all along, not added by the glass. Red, yellow and blue are only the painters' colours for mixing paint; sunlight holds every colour from red to violet.

Light can also be soaked up, or absorbed, and absorbed light turns into heat. Dark things absorb most of the light that falls on them, while white things reflect more of it away. So on a sunny day, a black T-shirt grows warmer than a white one, because it absorbs more of the sunlight. The air around both is just as warm. Lay a black cloth and a white one in the sun for an hour, then feel the difference for yourself.
